top_choice_rationale: P003 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) rewards one identifiable body of work. It supplies a common formal framework for how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy and economic performance. The core is about three decades old, so replication, extension and challenge have largely happened. Credit is concentrated, with the Persson-Tabellini pair at the centre and the Besley-Persson state-capacity strand as a separable second part. The 2024 institutions prize concerns the origins of institutions, a distinct object, so I treat proximity as a timing consideration rather than a scientific objection. The main cost is weaker cross-country identification, which the narrowed citation (a framework and its tests) acknowledges. P001 is second because its designs are the most checkable and its trio is tight, but its core results are only about a decade old and the Katz question is open. P002 (Kiyotaki-Moore) is third. It is mature and cleanly attributed, but marginal novelty relative to the 2022 prize is a concern and its aggregate evidence is indirect. P004 is fourth because the three-name cap cannot fairly represent a cumulative eight-name field and micro price evidence only partly supports the Calvo core. All four proposals are preferable to no award.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Persson, Tabellini or Besley. I disclose topical adjacency through my railroads and state-formation work with Johannes Lindvall and Alexandra Cermeño. I also disclose that Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund, with no stated co-authorship. My 2023 presentation speech and 2025 press role do not establish private preferences. As a dataset-building economic historian I may be sympathetic to the data contribution in P001, and I tried to weigh it evenly. Disclosure only, not a recusal.
